title: A CSV cell that parses as a harmless string can still execute as a formula the moment someone opens it in Excel
assumption: If a CSV parser reads a cell's value back as the exact literal string that was written, the value is safe wherever the file ends up.

input.description: User-controlled text (a name, a comment, an address) exported into a CSV/XLSX that will be opened by a human in Excel, Google Sheets, or LibreOffice Calc - any cell value beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` is a candidate formula to a spreadsheet application.

what_goes_wrong: A CSV writer/reader round-trips the attacker's string perfectly and faithfully - the field comes back exactly as `=cmd|' /C calc'!A0` - so nothing in the CSV layer looks wrong. But a spreadsheet application opening that same file treats any cell starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` as a formula to evaluate, which in older Excel versions could shell out via DDE (`cmd|...!A0`) or exfiltrate data to a remote URL through functions like `IMPORTXML` in Sheets - entirely outside what CSV parsing itself can see or prevent.
why: CSV has no concept of formulas; a cell is just delimited text. The danger is downstream: spreadsheet applications overload CSV as an import format for their own formula language, and that interpretation triggers on specific leading characters regardless of what the data "means" to your application. OWASP catalogs this as CSV Injection - the fix lives entirely on the writer side (how you emit values a spreadsheet will later open), because the CSV format and a conformant CSV parser are both working exactly as specified.
affects: any CSV exported for a human to open in a spreadsheet application

repros.code:
import csv, io

def sanitize(value):
    if isinstance(value, str) and value and value[0] in ("=", "+", "-", "@"):
        return "'" + value
    return value

payload = '=cmd|\' /C calc\'!A0'
raw = io.StringIO()
csv.writer(raw).writerow(["name", "amount"])
csv.writer(raw).writerow([payload, "100"])
print(repr(raw.getvalue()))
parsed = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(raw.getvalue())))
print(parsed[1][0] == payload)

safe = io.StringIO()
csv.writer(safe).writerow([sanitize(payload), "100"])
print(repr(safe.getvalue()))

fix: Prefix any user-controlled cell value that starts with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` (and, in some guidance, tab or carriage return) with a single quote or another neutralizing character before writing it to a file a human will open in a spreadsheet. Parsing the CSV correctly is necessary but not sufficient - the sanitization has to happen on write, aimed at the spreadsheet application's behavior, not the CSV format's.

sources.title: Python docs: csv - CSV File Reading and Writing

test_cases.note: A CSV-upload parser must return the cell exactly as written - the defence belongs on the export side (prefix values starting with =, +, -, @ with a single quote before writing a file a human will open in a spreadsheet), not in silently altering parsed data.
